title: Methods
summary: Define methods with parameters and return values, call them, overload them, accept a variable number of arguments, write recursive methods and understand pass-by-value.
introduction: A method is a named block of code that does one job: it takes inputs, does work and hands back a result. Methods let you reuse logic instead of copying it, give a readable name to a calculation, and test one piece of behaviour on its own. In this lesson you write static methods with parameters and return types, overload a method name for different inputs, accept any number of arguments, call a method from itself, and learn the rule that confuses most newcomers: Java always passes arguments by value, even when the value is a reference to an object.
learningObjectives: Define and call methods with parameters and return values
Overload a method name and use varargs for flexible argument lists
Explain what happens to primitives and object references passed to a method
Write a simple recursive method with a base case

blocks.text: A method declaration has a **return type** (or `void` when it returns nothing), a **name**, a parenthesised list of **parameters** with their types, and a body. Calling the method means writing its name with **arguments** in the same order as the parameters. The `static` keyword means the method belongs to the class rather than to an object; it is what lets `main`, which is itself static, call these methods directly. The [Classes and Objects](/tutorials/java/classes-objects) lesson introduces non-static methods.

blocks.text: `return` ends the method and hands the value to the caller, where it can be stored in a variable, printed, or used directly inside a larger expression such as `circleArea(1.0) > 3`. A `void` method may also use a bare `return;` to leave early. The compiler checks that every path through a non-void method reaches a `return`; if one is missing you get `error: missing return statement`.

Several methods may share a name as long as their **parameter lists** differ in number or types; this is **overloading**, and the compiler picks the version that matches the arguments best. A parameter declared with `...` (**varargs**) accepts zero or more values of that type and arrives inside the method as an array; it must be the last parameter.

blocks.title: Sums.java

blocks.text: `sum(2, 3)` matches the two-`int` version exactly, so the varargs version is not used even though it could accept the call; `sum(2.5, 3)` widens the `3` to a `double`; the four-argument and zero-argument calls can only mean the varargs version. The return type is **not** part of the choice: two methods that differ only in return type are a compile error.

When you call a method, Java **copies** each argument into the parameter. For a primitive the copy is the number itself, so reassigning the parameter never affects the caller's variable. For an object or array the copied value is the **reference**, the address of the object: the method can change the object's contents through that reference, and the caller sees those changes, but reassigning the parameter to a new object changes only the copy.

blocks.title: ByValue.java

blocks.text: `change` worked on a copy of `1`, so `x` is unchanged. `fill` followed the copied reference to the same array and overwrote slot 0, which the caller sees. `replace` pointed its own copy of the reference at a new array; the caller's `arr` still refers to the original. `Arrays.toString` from `java.util` is the convenient way to print an array's contents.

A method may call itself. Every recursive method needs a **base case** that returns without recursing, otherwise the calls never end and the JVM reports a `StackOverflowError`. Factorial is the classic example: `n!` is `n` times `(n - 1)!`, and `0!` and `1!` are `1`. The result type is `long` because factorials grow quickly; `20!` is the largest that fits.

blocks.title: Factorial.java

blocks.text: Variables declared inside a method, including its parameters, are **local**: they exist only while that call runs and are invisible to other methods. That isolation is the point; a method should receive what it needs through parameters and return its result rather than reaching into shared variables. Keep methods short, give them verb names that say what they do (`calculateTax`, `isEmpty`, `printReport`), and let each one do one thing. A method you can describe in one sentence is a method you can test.

blocks.title: Calling with the wrong types
blocks.text: Arguments must match the parameter types, and Java never guesses. Calling `circleArea("2")` with a string fails with `error: incompatible types: String cannot be converted to double`, and calling `sum(2, 3, 4)` on a class that only defines `sum(int, int)` fails with `error: method sum in class Sums cannot be applied to given types`. Read the message: it lists what was required and what was found.

questions.question: Assigning a new value to a parameter of type `int` inside a method changes the variable the caller passed in.
questions.explanation: Primitives are copied into the parameter. The method works on its own copy, so the caller's variable is untouched.

questions.question: What does javac report when an `int` method can reach its closing brace without executing a `return`?
questions.explanation: The compiler proves that every path returns a value. If some path does not, compilation stops with `missing return statement`; nothing is guessed at run time.
options: A warning, and the method returns null
A NullPointerException when the method is called
